> What if a vamp has E.S. on him (sup) and gets an aggravated, can he be

A slight clarification: Rotschreck is played before damage is dealt. By
the time he gets the agg, it's too late to play it.

But anyway, if you are trying to deal aggravated damage to a minion that
treats aggravated damage as normal, you can still play Rotschreck.

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
I considered creating a thread where everyone comes up with their own ban
lists, but that would get ugly, so I'll comment on yours.

>PTO

Does something no card should do. Ignoring all previous discussion as none of
it has done anything to change my view of the card, I see why it would be on
your list.

>Rotschreck

I've mellowed on my hostility towards this card. It's limited and, unlike a
lot of other things, it can be recovered from, at least a decent amount of the
time. I'm sure I could find cards that annoy me more. While it has weird
timing/interaction issues, I think there are other cards that cause similar
issues. Spirit Marionette, for example, would cover both complaints for me.

>Anarch Revolt

AR *decks* change the game into something not resembling what I picture a V:TES
game to be. Not much defense here except it would be easy to errata the card,
just annoying to add more errata to the game.

>Kindred Restructure
>Dramatic Upheaval

I might be persuaded that seat switching serves an important function in the
game in that it breaks up the predator-prey dynamic to a helpful degree as a
"hard" p-p-d is somehow bad. Might. Putting aside competitive play for a
moment, I often have these in hand in casual games and pitch them with the only
reason being that they are annoying to resolve. At the point where you think
you gain more from not annoying your friends than you do from trying to help
yourself to victory, the card(s) may exceed the obnoxious threshold. For
competitive play, what is most bothersome is the deck built around them that
totally skews the predator-prey dynamic. Still, V:TES (Jyhad) has always been
about many small effects and seat switching is not at all a small effect.

>DI

I'd rather that counterspells were never made. I'm annoyed by Sudden, but I'm
easy to convince that the game can't currently function without it. I probably
wouldn't put DI on my short list. It's stapleish, but so are lots of cards.
I've rarely seen it ruin games, more often stopping even more obnoxious plays
(than itself). Often, I'll have one in hand and not have a good use for it.
Maybe I just don't see it often enough in my opponents' hands (so to speak).

>In a radical world that would never exist, I would remove bounce from
>dominate entirely, creating an either/or scenario wrt bleed and bleed
>defense, but so far not a single person has agreed that that would be a
>good idea, so I'm probably nuts.

Suppose you give bounce to another discipline. Which? It would be pretty
funny to see Animalism be the primary bounce discipline, say. But, it might
cause Gangrel, who win *a lot* to be too powerful (admittedly, a lot of Gangrel
wins involve playing Dominate).

Anyway, while I'm often in the realm of "wish they had done that differently to
begin with", for today, why not just give everyone bounce? Is there any more
common element to decks than bounce? Its restriction to two disciplines
heavily skews what decks actually see play and which decks win more often.

At a minimum, if going to take baby steps, should be given to either a clan,
Assamite comes to mind, or a discipline like Celerity.

>__
>
>David Cherryholmes

They make enforcing playing to win impossible. And they are a pain in

Once again, not a card I'd ban from a play balance perspective.

>>DI
>
>
> I'd rather that counterspells were never made. I'm annoyed by Sudden, but I'm
> easy to convince that the game can't currently function without it. I probably
> wouldn't put DI on my short list. It's stapleish, but so are lots of cards.

> (than itself). Often, I'll have one in hand and not have a good use for it.
> Maybe I just don't see it often enough in my opponents' hands (so to speak).

Another card I approach from the perspective of re-enforcing the
predator-prey relationship. It's too easy for some guy across the table
to lob one of these out there, removing some linchpin card from a chain,
and oust another player. As the game stands, DI may be necessary, but
if it were more balanced as a whole we wouldn't need to suffer with DI.
I also dislike the way including four of these cards props up the
"moronic" bleed decks even further.

> Suppose you give bounce to another discipline. Which?

Auspex, and Auspex-like disciplines. It satisfies me that decks which
tend to lack means of going forward can utilize the forward motion
behind them. And yes, it means there would still be some bleeders that
can bounce, but if they deform their crypt such that the AUS is there,
and they tap and/or wake with every bounce, it would be sufficient to my
mind (note the heavy use of "IMO" throughout... I don't normally qualify
my opinions, but we are talking about sweeping changes I've yet to test).

> Anyway, while I'm often in the realm of "wish they had done that differently to
> begin with", for today, why not just give everyone bounce? Is there any more
> common element to decks than bounce? Its restriction to two disciplines
> heavily skews what decks actually see play and which decks win more often.

Everyone playing bounce seems worse to me than most everyone playing
bounce. I'd rather see it be an isolated strategy than a ubiquitous
one. Still, I think Xzealot captured it best when he said the answer
lies not in knocking down strategy X, but in making strategies Y and Z
more appealing; if stealth bleed were less clearly the most competitive
strategy, then the opportunity cost of bounce would rise, and things
might balance out without the need to change any staples.
Unfortunately, the (IMO) overly-conservative design strategy the game
currently operates under makes this approach either impossible, or
resolved in some distant future.

> At a minimum, if going to take baby steps, should be given to either a clan,
> Assamite comes to mind, or a discipline like Celerity.

Maybe, but it seems more and more plausible to me that the various clans
were never intended to be equal, and Assamites are placed rather low on
the food chain. The latest news of four !Gangrel, some of which are
group three, in the face of the Group 4 indy situation seems to suggest
this. Guess we'll see.

__

David Cherryholmes

available to "most everyone" instead of "very few". Or make better

have to be somewhat equally good answers.

played.

useful in moderation.

Jeroen Rombouts wrote:

> If this is the only reason, then Baltimore Purge and Smiling Jack should get
> the same treatment, for exactly the same reason.

Smiling Jack is unique, doesn't necessarily directly hit your pool, and
*much* easier to get rid of--it hits the table, does nothing for a full turn
around the table, then does 1 damage around the table, then does 2 damage
around the table. That is, what, 12 (not counting the guy who played it)
player turns of completely acceptible losses to get rid of it easily (i.e.
take an action that isn't blocked). If it lasts past that, everyone gets
what they ask for.

The damage is easier to absorb (you can lose blood off minions--when you are
in the 1-3 range of Jack, this is easy). The guy playing them *must* take
pool loss as opposed to blood loss. You can't play 2 of them a turn, every
turn. And taking an action to burn the single Jack on the table is *much*
easier than calling votes that might burn one of the 4 or 5 ARs on the table
at any given moment, especially when your game is completely compromised by
the large pool loss already caused by the ARs. And you get to see Jack
coming an react *before* it even does anything to anyone.

I have seen innumerable games savaged by AR decks. I have seen most Smiling
Jack decks either lose Jack before it hits 3 counters, or win the game, in
which case, the Jack deck isn't disruptive--it is successful.

Baltimore Purge, much like Jack, you can see coming. It is much easier to
stop (i.e. it isn't even at inherrent stealth, unless you are using a
Ravanos, in which case you don't get to choose the vampire, unless you are
playing a historically very effective Lasombra/Ravanos deck (???). And it
doesn't directly cause pool loss. And if someone plays lots and lots of
Baltimore Purges, everyone ends up in torpor, and the game simply stops.

Both of these cards certainly have a random element to them. But the amount
of effect on the game that their random elemet has is significantly less
that that of multiple Anarch Revolts. Very significantly.

do: you start a game, you've got a well-planned deck in a good position,
you've invested maybe a little more pool in your minions than usual but

position to defend against anything bad your predator and prey might want

Interesting. IMHO there are three instances when cards need to be
fixed.

1. Unbalanced. The card makes you win if you have it. IMHO currently
none of the cards fall into this category. Dreams may be a "must-have"
for most people, but the main reason I seldom play it is its
uniqueness. Many times were I gazing intently on my Dreams that
occupied my 7th slot and were unable to play it for countless turns,
as when one expired another one was played before my turn came.

2. Disruptive. The card makes other people lose (or be vastly
disappointed) by the card. Basically counter-cards are the ones that
could fall into this category. In VTES pulling a 6-card combo that
cannot be defended against is far less aggravating than playing a
single card. IMHO currently PTO is on the wrong side of the verge of
falling into this category. On the good side there is Judgement:
Camarilla Segregation and Goratrix, Advanced. They are far rarer
and/or less powerful.

3. Utterly Lame. Only thing that qualifies here is when two cards are
exactly the same in all but one effect parameter. The only current
example is Chainsaw vs. Gas Powered Chainsaw. Mario and Cristophero,
or Bastard Sword and Meat Cleaver do not count, as their effect
parameters match.

So in the current (IMHO rather fairly balanced) game I would change
exactly two cards. PTO (slightly balancing the effect to either allow
more dedicated defence or a decreased effect), and Chainsaw (by adding
a Maneuver and/or Press to the stike, for example, or decreasing the
cost / increasing the damage).

anarch/pool machine/major boon decks or what have you.

imo.

Bouncing to your grandpredator is underrated; it can be a good idea
even when you have Deflection, Redirection or Telepathic Misdirection.
No one else at the table will have a greater interest in blocking and
beating up the redirected bleeder. Also, no one has less of an
interest in returning the bleed to you, unless it is purely out of
spite. And at 5-person tables, killing your grandprey's prey is not a
disaster, since it stymies your prey and ups the pressure on your
predator.

Note also that MEE is more useful at 2- or 3-person tables than
Telepathic Misdirection. Since you're going to be at 2- or 3-person
tables more often than at 4- or 5-person tables (the endgame), MEE
looks pretty good.

> figure that you are the first person ousted 20-25%...

If you always play 5-person tables, and the odds of ousting are always
equal, you will be at a 3-person table in 60% of games and a 2-person
table in 40% of games.

If you always play 4-person tables, and the odds of ousting are always
equal, you will be at a 3-person table in 75% of games and a 2-person
table in 50% of games.

There's no available statistics on how many turns you're likely to
take while the game is at 4- or 5-players compared to while it is at
3- or 2-. However, your predator is likely to have more minions taking
actions for you to block or bounce in the late game.

Messages.Author: Izaak
Messages.Body:
I'm pretty sure that if you're going to give another discipline bounce,
you can make up a lot of examples of abuse.

That said, it's generally accepted that bounce is a nessecary evil.
Without bounce, it'd be all S/B. With it, AUS and dom have an inherent
"advantage" over the other disciplines. Otoh, on a combat table you'll
end up discarding deflections and in such situations it's for and cel
that have the inherent "advantage".

I don't think printing a new discipline-based bounce card is a bad idea.
All it would do is give a couple more clans access to in-clan bounce and
increase the frequency of that discipline (and the decks built with it).
As it stands, many people don't *want* to play dom or AUS all the time.
When the choice broadens to, say, dom, AUS, or obf you'll only end up
seeing more bounce and be even more fucked if you don't play bounce.

I think (and I already have suggested it a couple of times) that the
best idea to solve the "problem" is too look at bounce as a defensive
tool. Let's not forget that bounce is more offense than defense. Sure,
it saves you a couple of pool, but even better is that it hurts your
prey (generally) at the expense of an action of your predator. Win/win
situation if you ask me.

I still believe it'd be a good idea if there was a disciplineless bounce
card that bounced something back to the original target. Something like
this:

Confusing Orders
Reaction
1 blood
Do not replace until your next discard phase
Only usable on a bleed of more than 2 that's being redirected to you.
The acting minion is now bleeding the Methuselah that redirected the
bleed to you.
Tap this reacting minion.

ultimate bleed defense.

doesn't need the help, combat does.

longer.

vampires, now you also have to worry about your grand-predator's

and even midcaps -- weenies rule, otherwise. I think the game would've
been better with an innate effect, such as "Any vampire older than the
acting vampire may burn a blood to act as if untapped for the rest of
the action" or similar.

--Colin McGuigan

Generally not, no. Thankfully, there exist multiple options for how to
win games that do not include bouncing bleeds or rushing backwards.
Lots of decks win games and win tournaments with neither bounces nor
rushes. It's certainly an easy way to defend against the typical
stealth/bleed deck - no argument there.

But it's not a _necessity_ either, and you did use the (somewhat
garbled) sentence "Setites, Assamites, !Gangrel, !Nosferatu and
Nosferatu all
could need bounce" in your posts in this thread. My base point is that
in the case of (at least) one clan that you listed, they do not _need_
bounce, at all, to succeed.

> Wow, what an elaborate and thought out point! Obviously I am

> bounce a method to avoid getting bled to death, *without* having to go
> backwards all the time will unbalance the game *completely*! Horrors
> upon horrors, VTES would surely *die* if WW would try to even out the
> advantage Dominate and Auspex clans have over all the others!

Again, there are answers to 'don't get bled to death' besides bounce
or rushing backwards. For example, lots of decks use intercept instead
of bounce or rush. Lots of decks try to bloat faster than they lose
pool to bleeding. Lots of decks use votes to hamper bleeders or move
away from them on the table. Some decks even use bleed reduction
instead of bounce.

Perhaps more importantly, while stealth/bleed is one of the most
_basic_ decktypes, that doesn't make it the _dominant_ deck type these
days. (Anecdotal example: at the recent Qualifier for our region, four
of the five decks in the finals were not stealth bleed, and the fifth
was a hybrid stealth vote deck that did some secondary stealth
bleeding. The winning deck was an intercept-gun deck with 0 stealth
cards in it.)

Yes, I think that other clans and disciplines getting a way to bounce
would be helpful to them - I'm certainly not about to claim that it
would not.

But here's another point: your argument seems to be based entirely
around the fact that having a Bounce discipline available to you is an
advantage towards winning games for the clans that have it because
stealth/bleed is so powerful, and therefore should be addressed by
giving other clans that option as well.

But what's the difference between arguing that Celerity should have a
bounce card so that Celerity clans can keep up with Dom/Aus bounce,
and arguing that Potence should have a big stealth card so that
Potence clans can compete with Obf/Pro for ousting people via
stealth/bleed?

One of the absolute _core_ design points of every Vampire game WW has
made is that not all clans are equal in the details. Some of them are
better at certain tasks than the others, and every clan has things
they are bad at. That core diversity is a big reason why they _bother_
to have the concept of Clans in the first place, to make it so that
not every Vampire nor every Clan will be exactly the same when the
games are played.

Yes, some of the VTES clans are unbalanced and weaker than others
right now, and that's _definitely_ something a lot of players would
like to see resolved.

However, rather than resolve it by giving the weaker clans the exact
same (or carbon-copy) cards as the stronger clans, it would be much,
much better if they found ways to strengthen those clans in
_different_ ways, that maintain the diversity between the various
clans.

For example, in the Sabbat/Sabbat War period, very few people felt
_any_ of the Independent clans were competitive; they lacked way too
much to make them able to stand up to the Camarilla or Sabbat clans.
Instead of saying 'well, we'll make Independents have their own
Traditions' or 'we'll give the Setites lots of intercept and bounce
because they can't stop bleeds for squat', the designers made a bunch
of new cards that I'd like to think most players would agree helped
seriously address the imbalance of power levels. Things like Shambling
Hordes, Week of Nightmares, Clandestine Contract, Provision of the
Silisia, Enticement, Call the Hungry Dead, Free States Rant, etc etc.
Armed with a wide range of new strategies and options, the Independent
clans suddenly got played a _lot_ more often and easily, and did much,
much better in tournament play.

(Sadly, that significant boost to the independents didn't completely
rebalance the field; many people find the Assamites to still be very
weak in comparison.)

So rather than try to give similar-to-identical bounce options to the
clans/disciplines that are weaker for lacking that option, wouldn't it
be better to try to come up with _new_ and varied options and cards
for them, ones that will balance things overall without turning the
game into 'Vampire: Only The Names Are Different'?

> Magnus

-John Flournoy

SB does not rely on bouncing. It relies on bleeding at stealth. If
there is no bounce, you will need to (1) block, (2) bloat or (3) go
upstream.

(1) If you pack enough intercept to reliably block a SB you will die
horribly when anything that is not stealth-heavy sits behind you.

we're talking about a game that is supposedly playable with many
different concepts.

till a point. It does not, however, win you games.

consequences of their actions. A bleed for six at stealth may easily
turn out to give your prey +6 pool instead of -6. Not to mention the
VP lost (that could have been gained).

Bounce is cool for the game. Without it, the game would be even more
about SB vs. Anti-SB.

...and if it isn't, it isn't likely to be doing me much good. I think
the trouble is, we disagree on what kind of an effort this represents.
I think calling a +1 stealth vote on an effect that is generally
unpopular is a superbly easy thing to do. I notice you pushing the
concept that the owner's deck might have reactions, wakes, and nasty
combat as a drawback to sweeping the card. But that kind of stuff is a
whole strategy unto itself, with not insignificant costs. (For instance,
packing all that defense inevitably weakens one's ousting ability.) If
that's the kind of strategy a player wishes to pursue, there's much
BETTER stuff to be sticking on the table to defend and even tempt opposing
players with than a card that costs everyone pool equally beginning with
you. Powerbase: Montreal, The Rack, and Smiling Jack all come to mind.
(And, of course, you then start throwing out Millicent Smith since you
don't like actions and are comfortable not acting yourself.) Master
card space in such decks, as I continually point out, needs to be
consumed by much better master cards. Assuming one is playing to win,
of course.
>
> > I will NOT give you that.
>
> Umm, Ok. You should still probably settle down some.

And you should probably dim your lighting further, put on another
Yanni album, and try not to let it bother you. The throbbing vein on
my forehead doesn't burst very often and when it does, the blood
gushing all over is surprisingly easy to clean up.

(Usenet. Cripes.)

> > If you can't get the votes, it's usually because the thing is
> > *SO* insignificant, it's off peoples' radar screens. In which case it
> > was a waste of master phase.
>
> To make your prey lose pool. Hardly a waste for my money. But, ya know, me.

And his prey and you and everyone else. It you want to cover your eyes
and look at only the good part of the picture, I make anything look
good. Root canal work gets you off your feet for a couple of hours,
don't you know? However, it's my belief that understanding about such
things requires one to look at the big picture. Most of the objections
to the points I've made in this thread seem to be based on people failing
to do that.

> Sometimes the actions spent going forward are worth more than
> the saving of the pool from the AR. If this isn't the case, then
> the AR gets killed. If not, it stays around and speeds up the game.

...freeing up time for the aforementioned root canal work. What with
the adjustment you're proposing for the card, certainly its user need
not fear having to hang around too long.

> There are certainly worse expenditures of master phase actions.

Sure. As long things like Brainwash exist, there certainly are. I
could even target my own locations with Unnatural Disasters, getting
myself coming and going. However, if one wants to look there will
almost inevitably be much _better_ expenditures of master phase
actions - which I think is more the point.

> > Just that your proposed solution basically does the first thing you said:
> > removes it from the game completely. A coaster is a dead card in a CCG.
>
> Ok. Then it possibly isn't the best solution to the problem. I never said it
> was the best possible option. Just an option.

OK, good. Because then we get to Wouter Kuyper was trying to make to you:
about whether it's even an option that's better than leaving things alone.
I doubt we'll make headway on that one, however. It depends on how much
pain you feel the card causes, which is a pretty subjective thing.

> > You may have observed people doing it. But it's a stupid play. Presumedly,
> > one would expect such people to prefer Anteduluvian Awakening to AR. You've
> > said nothing about people using AA first and then using AR as a fallback
> > because they can't use more than one AA. But then, that would contradict
> > your suggestion that anyone want more than one or two in play. The first
> > one, by all accounts, should Anteduluvian Awakening.
>
> Maybe. But Antedulivan is Unique. So playing more than 1 is counter
> productive, if you might want to play 2 of them. So you put in an
> Antedeluvian and a few ARs. 1 AA is interchangable with 1 AR for most
> purposes.

Not really. The removal cost on the AA makes it much more desirable to
use, for the first one. Since you're claiming that the use of the
modified AR would involve only one or two of them being on the table at
a time, there's almost no reason to use them. Use AA instead. You'll
be limited to one on the table at a time but that basically fulfills the
use you're talking about putting AR to and is the far superior way to do
it.

Fred

Well, what you exactly said (in context):

>> Without bounce, it'd be all S/B.
>
> Actually, no. Yes, one less defense against S+B, but since S+B tends to
> play with bounce _anyways_, I don't think there'd be a dominance effect.

This implies that SB relies on bounce. Which is far from the truth.

> > Bounce is cool for the game. Without it, the game would be even more
> > about SB vs. Anti-SB.
>
> With bounce, the game becomes (for the S+B predator) "Does my prey have
> bounce in his hand or not?" If he does, the S+B loses -- it can do jack
> else. If he doesn't, the S+B wins.

The salt and pepper of playing S&B is that there are strategies to
counter it. Otherwise paying around 5 pool for a vampire who will
cause about 5 pool loss to my prey *every turn* is just too good. Good
enough to trump other decks.

Bounce is the pillar of S&B defence. Not only does it protect the
player from the bleed, but it also allows him to use the momentum of
his predator against his prey. Meaning, an irresposible bleeder will
likely win the table for his well-prepared prey.

> Not seeing the improvement.

None is needed. Bounce helps to keep S&B in check. So does AI. Many
bleed decks do bleeds for 3 at sufficient stealth with a Spying
mission in hand. Even against a prey who does not use bounce or AI.
Because those countermeasures are considered during deck construction.
Their mere existance keeps bleed decks in check.
